prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: It’s alot like

outputs.L1:
It is rather like a cave filled with pictures and black-and-white checkered flags, and one might easily overdose on caffeine there. It is the closest restaurant to our house—perhaps five miles away—and it is very inexpensive, the sort of place you can visit when you have almost no money. They let you use the telephone. I can get steak tartare there for $2.25, though I have never called it that; to me it is simply raw hamburger with an egg yolk, pickle relish, garlic powder, and the Celtic salt I bring along.

The owner, H—after whom the H-burger is named—is loquacious and surprising, with a Santa Claus belly and suspenders. There are ashtrays everywhere and a wonderful old pinball machine. It feels like East Nassau, though it is in West Lebanon. I think you can always talk there about the weather and hunting. The clientele is open-minded, as are the waitress and the waiter, who kneels when he takes your order. During hunting season, it opens at 4:30 a.m. It is for sale, though not entirely seriously. H’s wife thinks he spends too much time there—which he does—so she has started calling him by their dog’s name, Peaches. H is a great fan of *Northern Exposure*. Oh, and I forgot to mention the biscuits and sausage gravy, which are genuine, grayish, and great. Recently, H got a smoker, and this year we will go to the New Year’s Eve party and eat stuffed shrimp and/or lobster.
outputs.L2:
It feels very much like being inside a cave covered with pictures and black-and-white checkered flags. You could probably drink enough coffee there to overdo it. It’s the nearest restaurant to our place, roughly five miles away, and it’s inexpensive enough that you can eat there even when you’re nearly broke. They’ll let you use the phone, too.

For $2.25, I can order what would technically be steak tartare, though I’ve never called it that—just raw hamburger topped with an egg yolk, pickle relish, garlic powder, and the Celtic salt I bring with me. The owner, H, whose name is behind the “H-burger,” talks a lot, is full of surprises, has a Santa-like stomach, and wears suspenders.

Ashtrays are scattered all over, and there’s a wonderful old pinball machine. The place feels as though it belongs in East Nassau, even though it’s actually in West Lebanon. The weather and hunting are always safe topics of conversation. The customers are broad-minded, and so are the waitress and the waiter, who gets down on one knee to take your order. During hunting season, the restaurant opens at 4:30 in the morning.

The place is technically up for sale, although not in any very serious way. H’s wife believes he spends far too much time there—which he does—so she has begun calling him by the name of their dog, Peaches. H loves *Northern Exposure*. I should also mention the biscuits with sausage gravy: authentic, grayish, and excellent. Lately H bought a smoker, and this year we’re planning to go to the New Year’s Eve party there and have stuffed shrimp and/or lobster.
outputs.L3:
The restaurant is close enough to feel like an extension of the neighborhood, the kind of place one can drift into without planning and leave with the sense of having found something oddly memorable. It is also remarkably cheap, almost unbelievably so, and its low prices are part of its charm. Inside, the atmosphere is distinctive: dim, enclosed, and cave-like, with black-and-white flags hanging about, ashtrays still present as if from another era, and an old pinball machine adding to the feeling that the place has resisted change in the best possible way.

The food is one of the narrator’s great pleasures. For very little money, it is possible to eat surprisingly well: steak tartare offered at a price that seems almost impossible, biscuits with sausage gravy, stuffed shrimp, and even lobster. The menu has the comforting range of a place that knows its customers and is not interested in pretending to be fashionable. It serves food that is generous, satisfying, and unexpectedly good.

Much of the restaurant’s character comes from its owner, H. He is talkative, unpredictable, and full of surprises, the sort of person who can turn an ordinary visit into a story. He wears suspenders and seems inseparable from the place, as if the restaurant is not simply his business but his true home. His attachment is so complete that his wife jokes about it, teasing him for being more devoted to the restaurant than to anything else.

The people who gather there help create its welcoming atmosphere. The clientele and staff are open-minded and easygoing, making the restaurant feel accessible rather than exclusive. Conversations tend to follow familiar local rhythms, often circling around the weather, hunting, and whatever else happens to be on people’s minds. It is a place where talk comes easily, and where strangers do not necessarily remain strangers for long.

During hunting season, the restaurant opens very early, ready to serve hunters before dawn. Although it is technically for sale, it continues to function as a lively community space, hosting events such as a New Year’s Eve party and maintaining its role as a local gathering place. Its future may be uncertain, but for now it remains exactly what it has long been: inexpensive, welcoming, eccentric, and full of life.
outputs.L4:
The restaurant is only a short walk from my house, tucked between a laundromat and a small convenience store, and from the outside it does not look like much. Its sign is faded, one corner of the awning droops slightly, and the front window is crowded with handwritten notices advertising lunch specials, homemade soup, and “best coffee in town.” Still, there is something inviting about it. At almost any hour, the place glows warmly from within, and the smell of frying onions, strong coffee, and fresh bread drifts out whenever someone opens the door.

Inside, the restaurant is wonderfully odd. Nothing matches, but somehow everything belongs. The tables are covered with plastic cloths in different patterns, the chairs look as if they were collected from yard sales over the past thirty years, and the walls are packed with old photographs, postcards, sports pennants, children’s drawings, and a clock shaped like a rooster that does not seem to keep the correct time. Near the counter sits a glass case full of pies, each one labeled in thick black marker. A small radio plays quietly in the kitchen, usually competing with the hum of conversation and the clatter of plates.

The food is simple, cheap, and deeply satisfying. This is not the kind of restaurant where anyone discusses presentation or trendy ingredients. It serves thick pancakes, greasy eggs, hot sandwiches, meatloaf, mashed potatoes, soup, burgers, fries, and slices of pie big enough to make lunch feel like a holiday. The coffee is always refilled before the cup is empty, and the portions are generous enough that people often leave carrying a foil-wrapped bundle for later. Nothing on the menu costs very much, which is part of the restaurant’s charm. It is one of the few places where a person can sit down, eat a full meal, and not feel punished by the bill.

The owner is as much a part of the restaurant as the stove or the front counter. He is usually there, moving between the kitchen and the dining room, greeting regulars by name and asking after their children, their jobs, their dogs, or their aching knees. He has a dry sense of humor and a habit of pretending to be gruff, but everyone knows he is kind. If someone is short a few dollars, he waves it away. If a customer has not come in for a while, he notices. He seems to know every story in the neighborhood and, if asked, will gladly tell most of them.

The staff share the same no-nonsense warmth. The waitresses are quick, practical, and affectionate in a teasing way. They call people “hon,” remember who wants extra butter, and can carry four plates at once while still keeping track of which table needs ketchup. They are not overly formal, and that is part of why the place feels comfortable. A newcomer may be surprised at first by the joking and familiar tone, but after a few visits it begins to feel less like service and more like being folded into a routine that has existed for years.

The customers are a mixture of nearly everyone in the area. Early in the morning, older men sit at the counter reading newspapers and discussing local politics as if they are running the town. At lunchtime, construction workers, office clerks, students, delivery drivers, and parents with small children fill the tables. In the afternoon, retired neighbors linger over coffee, and in the evening families come in for inexpensive dinners. People who might not meet anywhere else end up sitting side by side here, sharing the same noise, warmth, and smell of fried potatoes.

What makes the restaurant special is not perfection. In fact, much of its appeal comes from its imperfections. The floor creaks, the menus are slightly sticky, and one of the booths has a rip carefully repaired with silver tape. Sometimes the service is slow when the place is crowded, and sometimes the soup runs out before noon. But these flaws only make the restaurant feel more human. It has personality, history, and a kind of stubborn independence that newer, shinier places often lack.

The atmosphere is lively but relaxed, eccentric but welcoming. People do not come here to be impressed; they come to be fed, recognized, and comforted. The restaurant offers something increasingly rare: a public place that still feels personal. It is cheap without being careless, strange without being alienating, and familiar without becoming dull. For the neighborhood, it is more than a convenient place to eat. It is a meeting point, a refuge, a source of gossip, a breakfast habit, and a small shared treasure.

In the end, the restaurant’s value cannot be measured only by its menu or prices, though both are important. Its real worth lies in the way it gathers people together. It gives the neighborhood a place to sit down, warm up, talk, laugh, and feel at home. It may be quirky, crowded, and a little worn around the edges, but that is exactly why it is beloved. It has character, and in a world of polished chains and expensive cafés, character is worth a great deal.
outputs.L5:
It’s alot like standing at the edge of something new and realizing that change can feel both exciting and uncertain. At first, everything may seem unfamiliar, but with time, small steps begin to make the path clearer. Whether it is learning a new skill, starting a different routine, or facing an unexpected challenge, the experience often teaches patience, confidence, and resilience.

It’s alot like planting a seed. You may not see results immediately, but with care, effort, and consistency, growth begins to happen. The important thing is to keep going, even when progress feels slow. Every effort matters, and every lesson adds value to the journey.

In the end, life is full of moments that test us and shape us. It’s alot like a story that continues to unfold, one chapter at a time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single long, lowercase, stream-of-consciousness paragraph describing a quirky cheap roadside restaurant near home, with specific details about the food, owner, regulars, decor, and atmosphere.
counterfactuals.output: there’s this cheap little roadside restaurant near my house that everyone just calls “the blue shed,” even though the paint has faded into a kind of tired grayish turquoise and half the sign is missing, and it sits right beside the bus stop where the road dips and puddles gather after rain, with a plastic menu board out front listing tea, egg rolls, lentil soup, fried rice, potato curry, and “special noodles” in crooked red letters, though the special noodles are only special because mr. basu, the owner, tosses in whatever vegetables are left in the fridge and somehow makes it taste smoky and salty and perfect, especially when he adds too much green chili and then laughs like it was an accident; he is a thin man with a white mustache, a wool cap no matter the weather, and a habit of wiping every plate with the same blue towel while telling customers that the world has gone downhill since people stopped eating breakfast properly, and his wife, who everyone calls auntie mina, sits near the cash box in the corner counting coins, scolding him, and secretly giving extra gravy to schoolchildren and tired delivery drivers; the food is greasy in the honest way, the kind that shines under the buzzing tube light, with parathas stacked in a dented steel box, omelets folded around onions and cilantro, chickpea stew bubbling in a blackened pot, tea served in thick little glasses that burn your fingers, and a mysterious red sauce that tastes like tomato, garlic, sugar, and trouble, and there are always the same regulars: the retired postman who reads yesterday’s newspaper as if it might change, two mechanics with oil-black hands who argue about cricket, a woman who sells flowers and eats silently by the door, three college boys sharing one plate of fries and pretending they are not broke, and an old dog named biscuit who sleeps under the bench until someone drops a piece of bread; inside, the walls are covered with calendars from different years, a cracked mirror, a poster of a mountain waterfall, a plastic clock that runs ten minutes fast, and strings of dusty fake marigolds hanging above the counter, while the chairs wobble, the tables have carved initials and sauce stains shaped like countries, and the ceiling fan makes a clicking sound that becomes part of the music along with the radio hissing old songs, scooters passing outside, spoons clinking against steel plates, and mr. basu shouting “one more tea, less sugar, more ginger” even when nobody asked, and the whole place smells of frying oil, wet earth, cardamom, exhaust, and warm bread, and somehow, despite the chipped cups and the sticky floor and the fact that the napkins are always cut-up newspaper, it feels softer than home on certain evenings, like the restaurant is a small noisy pocket in the world where everybody is allowed to be hungry, tired, strange, and still welcome.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose-poem restaurant review in the style of an eccentric rural New England diary entry, mentioning raw hamburger with egg yolk, hunting season, ashtrays, pinball, biscuits and sausage gravy, and a talkative owner named h.
counterfactuals.output:
November 13, hard frost on the pasture, maples gone black at the edges.

Stopped at the little roadside place by the bend where the trucks idle like old bears and the screen door slaps its opinion into the room. Hunting season has set every man in orange to speaking softly of deer, as if the woods were a church and not a place full of burrs and bad luck. Inside: ashtrays on the tables, real ones, heavy as moral judgment; a pinball machine in the corner flashing its tiny carnival gospel; coffee thick enough to mend a boot.

The owner, called only **h**, was talkative in the manner of a brook after rain. Told me about the roof, the town, the price of onions, a cousin with a useless dog, and the old days when folks still knew how to order without staring at a wall of choices. I ordered anyhow.

First came raw hamburger with egg yolk, bright as a harvest moon set down in a red field. Not pretty, exactly, but earnest—salt, pepper, onion, a dare from another century. Then biscuits and sausage gravy, pale and mountainous, the sort of meal that puts its hand on your shoulder and says: stay through winter. The biscuits were tender, the gravy peppered with enough authority to make a minister blink.

This is not fine dining. Fine dining would faint here. This is a place with mud on its cuffs, where breakfast and supper have not been properly introduced, where the pinball bells go off like sleigh bells in a fever, and h keeps talking until you feel you’ve either married into the town or been deputized.

Four stars, maybe five if the stove holds out. I left full, smoky, and strangely forgiven.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe “H’s” diner in West Lebanon as if recalling it to a friend: make it rambling, funny, intimate, and full of odd details like checked flags, caffeine, steak tartare for $2.25, a kneeling waiter, and New Year’s Eve lobster.
counterfactuals.output:
Oh, H’s diner in West Lebanon — you would have loved it, or hated it, which is nearly the same thing with places like that. It had that exhausted little roadside glamour, you know? The kind that looks as if it was assembled out of chrome, frying oil, bad weather, and somebody’s optimism from 1947.

There were checked flags everywhere — not real flags exactly, more like the idea of flags, black-and-white racing checks on the walls, on the menus, maybe even in the waitress’s soul. Everything seemed to be waving you toward speed while the service itself moved with the solemn pace of a funeral in mud season. The coffee was not coffee so much as a civic duty: black, hot, bottomless, and with that peculiar diner bitterness that makes you feel you’ve been awake since the Truman administration. I drank so much of it my elbows began to hum.

And the menu! My God, the menu. It had the usual sturdy American promises — hamburgers, ham steaks, eggs at all hours, pie under glass looking slightly accused — and then, tucked in among the grilled cheese and the meat loaf, there it was: **steak tartare, $2.25**. Steak tartare! In West Lebanon! For two dollars and twenty-five cents! The very phrase sat there on the page wearing a monocle. I kept staring at it, wondering who ordered raw beef in a roadside diner beneath checked flags, and whether that person later married well or died young.

The waiter — do you remember I told you about the waiter? — at one point actually knelt beside the table. Not in a romantic way, not quite, and not because he’d dropped anything. He just sank down beside us, one knee on the floor, pad in hand, as if taking confession from two sinners who couldn’t decide between the club sandwich and the Salisbury steak. It was intimate and alarming. I wanted to tell him everything: my order, my regrets, my mother’s maiden name.

The whole place had that democratic diner clatter: spoons ringing in thick white mugs, somebody laughing too loudly in a booth, the kitchen door flapping like an irritated mouth. There was a man at the counter eating pie with the fixed concentration of a safecracker. A woman near the window kept reapplying lipstick between sips of coffee, as though preparing to be discovered. Outside, cars came and went with wet tires and brief headlights, and inside we sat in the yellow light, caffeinated and ridiculous, feeling somehow both stranded and perfectly provided for.

And then there was the sign about **New Year’s Eve lobster**. I swear to you: lobster, festive lobster, celebratory lobster, in that place of coffee fumes and checked flags and bargain tartare. I pictured everyone there at midnight with paper hats sliding over one eye, cracking shells under fluorescent light, butter running down their wrists, someone’s aunt crying quietly into coleslaw. It seemed both tragic and magnificent — which is probably the highest form of American dining.

Anyway, H’s was one of those places you don’t really “eat at” so much as survive briefly and then remember forever. I can’t tell you if the food was good. That’s not the category. It was *there*. It had confidence. It had caffeine. It had steak tartare for $2.25 and a kneeling waiter and holiday lobster advertised like a miracle. What more can a person reasonably ask from West Lebanon?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a quirky first-person vignette about the closest restaurant to someone’s house, very cheap and open early for hunters, with a Santa-bellied owner in suspenders, a smoker, and a clientele that talks about weather and hunting.
counterfactuals.output:
The closest restaurant to my house is the kind of place you don’t so much “go to” as get absorbed by, like woodsmoke into a flannel shirt.

It opens at some punishing hour designed for hunters, insomniacs, and men who believe breakfast should happen while the moon is still on duty. The sign in the window says OPEN in red neon, but it feels less like an invitation and more like a lantern hung outside a cave.

Inside, everything is cheap enough to make you suspicious. Coffee costs less than a parking meter. Eggs arrive in pairs, glossy and obedient. The toast is buttered with the confidence of a place that has never heard of cholesterol and wouldn’t respect it if it had.

The owner is shaped exactly like Santa Claus after a summer of fixing tractors: big white beard, red cheeks, belly pushing proudly against suspenders that look like they’ve held the line in several small wars. He keeps a smoker out back, and by six in the morning the whole restaurant smells like hickory, bacon grease, and somebody’s grandfather telling the truth.

I sit at the counter because that’s where the regulars can inspect me without turning their heads. They wear camouflage even when they’re not hunting, as if the deer might wander in for pancakes and need to be fooled. They talk weather with the seriousness of diplomats.

“Frost by Friday,” one says.

“Too damp for tracking,” says another.

“Wind’s wrong,” says a third, and everyone nods as though the wind has a long history of making poor decisions.

Now and then someone mentions a buck so large it sounds mythological, like it should have antlers made of lightning and its own ZIP code.

The owner refills my coffee without asking. His suspenders creak. Somewhere out back, the smoker exhales like a dragon with a side hustle.

And because it’s close, and cheap, and open before the sun has put its face on, I keep ending up there—half awake, smelling like smoke, listening to men judge the sky.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an unpolished, run-on review of a beloved local dive restaurant, using ampersands, minimal capitalization, and vivid specifics about its decor, food, staff, owner’s wife, telephone, pinball machine, and greyish sausage gravy.
counterfactuals.output: i love this place more than is probably reasonable & it looks like it was decorated by a fishing uncle, a retired bowling team, and somebody’s grandma all arguing at once, there’s wood paneling, crooked beer signs, a dusty plastic fern over the pie cooler, a deer head wearing mardi gras beads, and the same red vinyl booths with little tape patches that stick to your elbow in july, the food is cheap & hot & exactly what you want, eggs over easy sliding into hash browns, burgers wrapped in wax paper, toast with too much butter, coffee that tastes like it’s been on since 1998 but in a good way, and yes the greyish sausage gravy looks like wet cement with pepper in it but it is honestly perfect, salty & thick & weirdly comforting over biscuits that are never fancy but always gone in 4 minutes, the waitress calls everybody hon even when she’s mad, the cook yells “order up” like he’s announcing a house fire, the owner wanders around in a ball cap pretending he’s not keeping track of every single regular, and the owner’s wife is the real boss, she’s usually by the register with her readers on a chain, answering that ancient beige telephone with the curly cord like it’s mission control, telling suppliers no, seating families, refilling napkins, scolding somebody’s kid, and somehow knowing who needs extra gravy before they ask, there’s a pinball machine in the corner that only half works & the left flipper sticks unless you smack the side just right, which everyone does even though there’s a handwritten sign saying don’t hit machine, and honestly if you want stainless steel brunch with microgreens go somewhere else, but if you want a plate that could fix a hangover, a bad mood, or a broken heart for $8.95, this is the place, five stars, bring cash, don’t sit in frank’s booth unless you’re frank.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
